The Messiah's righteous and peaceful kingdom (verses 1–9)

The Messiah is called a Rod and a Branch, terms suggesting a small, delicate shoot that might easily be broken.

He grows from Jesse's stem, after David's royal family has been cut down and brought almost to the ground.

By the time Jesus was born, that house had sunk very low.

His humble beginning showed that his kingdom was not of this world.

The Holy Spirit rests upon him, with every gift and grace.

The fullness of deity dwells in him (Colossians 1:19; 2:9).

Henry notes that many readers recognize seven gifts of the Spirit in this description, and sees the passage as clearly teaching the Spirit's work.

The Messiah governs with perfect justice and righteousness.

He accomplishes his judgments by his word and Spirit.

Great peace belongs to his kingdom.

The gospel transforms human nature. Those who once oppressed gentle people become gentle and kind themselves.

This transformation has appeared throughout Christian history, although it awaits a far fuller manifestation in the latter days.

As the great Shepherd, Christ cares for his flock and changes the significance of suffering and death so thoroughly that these things cannot do his people ultimate harm.

God's people are freed not only from evil itself but also from the fear of it.

Who can separate them from Christ's love?

As we grow in the knowledge of the God of love, we become more like him and more loving toward those who bear his likeness.

Knowledge of the Lord will spread as widely as the sea extends.

Christians in every age have witnessed something of this blessed power, though the most glorious fulfillment remains ahead.

Meanwhile, let us live and work in ways that honor Christ and his kingdom of peace.

The Gentiles and Israel gathered to Christ (verses 10–16)

When the gospel is openly preached, Gentiles will seek Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior and find rest for their souls.

When the Lord's time arrives to deliver his people, even mountains of opposition become level ground before him.

He can quickly change dark days into glorious ones.

Henry looks forward to the Lord gathering his ancient people into the church, along with the fullness of the Gentiles, so that all may be united in holy love.

Until that time, let us follow the highway of holiness prepared for the redeemed.

Wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ unto eternal life.

Trust him to prepare the way through death, the river separating this world from eternity.

Verses 1-9 The Messiah is called a Rod, and a Branch. The words signify a small, tender product; a shoot, such as is easily broken off. He comes forth out of the stem of Jesse; when the royal family was cut down and almost levelled with the ground, it would sprout again. The house of David was brought very low at the time of Christ's birth. The Messiah thus gave early notice that his kingdom was not of this world. But the Holy Spirit, in all his gifts and graces, shall rest and abide upon him; he shall have the fulness of the Godhead dwelling in him, [Col.1.19] Col. 1:19; 2:9. Many consider that seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are here mentioned. And the doctrine of the influences of the Holy Spirit is here clearly taught. The Messiah would be just and righteous in all his government. His threatening shall be executed by the working of his Spirit according to his word. There shall be great peace and quiet under his government. The gospel changes the nature, and makes those who trampled on the meek of the earth, meek like them, and kind to them. But it shall be more fully shown in the latter days. Also Christ, the great Shepherd, shall take care of his flock, that the nature of troubles, and of death itself, shall be so changed, that they shall not do any real hurt. God's people shall be delivered, not only from evil, but from the fear of it. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? The better we know the God of love, the more shall we be changed into the same likeness, and the better disposed to all who have any likeness to him. This knowledge shall extend as the sea, so far shall it spread. And this blessed power there have been witnesses in every age of Christianity, though its most glorious time, here foretold, is not yet arrived. Meanwhile let us aim that our example and endeavours may help to promote the honour of Christ and his kingdom of peace.
[Isa.11.10-Isa.11.16]
Verses 10-16 When the gospel should be publicly preached, the Gentiles would seek Christ Jesus as their Lord and Saviour, and find rest of soul. When God's time is come for the deliverance of his people, mountains of opposition shall become plains before him. God can soon turn gloomy days into glorious ones. And while we expect the Lord to gather his ancient people, and bring them home to his church, also to bring in the fulness of the Gentiles, when all will be united in holy love, let us tread the highway of holiness he has made for his redeemed. Let us wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life, looking to him to prepare our way through death, that river which separates this world from the eternal world.

modern_osis:
Original heading

This is a hymn of praise suited to the times of the Messiah.

A song of salvation and thanksgiving

This song would be fitting when Israel's exiles finally returned from their long captivity.

It is especially fitting when a sinner first discovers peace and joy through faith.

It also belongs to believers whose peace is renewed after God's correction for past wandering, and to all the redeemed together before God's throne in heaven.

The promise is certain and its blessings abundant.

Everything received through Jesus Christ calls us to wholehearted thanksgiving.

Through Jesus Christ, the Root of Jesse, divine anger was turned away, because he is our Peace.

Those whom God has reconciled to himself receive his comfort.

They learn to rejoice in him and in the assurance that they belong to him.

Let the believer say: I will trust God to prepare me for his salvation and keep me until its full realization.

I will entrust every concern to him, confident that he can make all things work together for good.

Faith in God is a powerful remedy against tormenting fears.

Many Christians know God as their strength but fail to make him their song.

They remain in spiritual darkness and miss the joy that should accompany their confidence.

Those who rely upon his strength ought to praise him for it, giving him the glory and accepting the comfort.

Salvation arises from God the Father's love, reaches us through God the Son, and is applied by the renewing power of God the Spirit.

When faith sees this, the frightened sinner learns to hope in God and loses the fear that formerly enslaved the soul.

The purifying and sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit is often pictured as water springing from a fountain.

This grace comes through Christ's mediation and is conveyed to our souls through God's appointed means of worship and instruction.

Praise God that wells of salvation are open on every side, from which we may draw living water and consolation.

In the latter part of the song (verses 4–6), believers urge one another to praise the Lord and invite still more people to join them.

Disagreements about dates, seasons and other secondary matters must not divide Christian hearts.

Our deepest concern should be to belong among those to whom Christ will finally say:

“Come, you who are blessed by my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

[Isa.12.1]
Chapter 12
This is a hymn of praise suited to the times of the Messiah.
The song of praise in this chapter is suitable for the return of the outcasts of Israel from their long captivity, but it is especially suitable to the case of a sinner, when he first finds peace and joy in believing; to that of a believer, when his peace is renewed after corrections for backslidings; and to that of the whole company of the redeemed, when they meet before the throne of God in heaven. The promise is sure, and the blessings contained in it are very rich; and the benefits enjoyed through Jesus Christ, call for the most enlarged thanksgivings. By Jesus Christ, the Root of Jesse, the Divine anger against mankind was turned away, for he is our Peace. Those to whom God is reconciled, he comforts. They are taught to triumph in God and their interest in him. I will trust him to prepare me for his salvation, and preserve me to it. I will trust him with all my concerns, not doubting but he will make all to work for good. Faith in God is a sovereign remedy against tormenting fears. Many Christians have God for their strength, who have him not for their song; they walk in darkness: but those who have God for their strength ought to make him their song; that is, give him the glory of it, and take to themselves the comfort of it. This salvation is from the love of God the Father, it comes to us through God the Son, it is applied by the new-creating power of God the Spirit. When this is seen by faith, the trembling sinner learns to hope in God, and is delivered from fear. The purifying and sanctifying influences of the Holy Ghost often are denoted under the emblem of springing water. This work flows through the mediation of Christ, and is conveyed to our souls by means of God's ordinances. Blessed be God, we have wells of salvation opened on every side, and may draw from them the waters of life and consolation. In the second part of this gospel song, [Isa.12.4-Isa.12.6] Is. 12:4-6, believers encourage one another to praise God, and seek to draw others to join them in it. No difference of opinions about the times and seasons, and other such matters, ought to divide the hearts of Christians. Let it be our care that we may be placed amongst those to whom he will say, Come, ye blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.

The appointed armies of judgment (verses 1–5)

Warnings from God's word become a heavy burden to those determined to remain wicked.

The forces gathered against Babylon are called God's consecrated or appointed ones because they are designated for this particular work and given the ability to accomplish it.

They are also called his mighty ones, for even their strength comes from him.

They would arrive from distant lands.

God can bring judgment through people who seem so far away that no one imagines they might ever become dangerous.

Babylon's defeat by the Medes and Persians (verses 6–18)

Isaiah describes Babylon's terrible overthrow by the Medes and Persians.

People who were arrogant, cruel and frightening during prosperity can become overwhelmed by terror when calamity arrives.

Every confidence and comfort would fail.

The sun and stars are described as losing their light.

Such language often appears in the prophets to picture the upheaval of governments and kingdoms.

God would confront Babylon's wrongdoing, especially pride, which brings people low.

The destruction is pictured as a general scene of horror.

Those who join themselves to Babylon should expect to share her judgments (Revelation 18:4).

People are willing to surrender all their possessions to preserve life, yet their wealth cannot ransom them from death.

The cruelty described here should make us grieve and wonder how deeply human nature has become corrupted.

Henry also addresses the suffering of infants. He connects the reality of death from life's very beginning with his doctrine of humanity's inherited guilt through the fall.

That is his theological explanation of the tragedy, not an endorsement of brutality.

The final day of the Lord will be more terrible still than the judgments described in this chapter.

The unrepentant will find no refuge.

Yet few people behave as though they believe these warnings.

Babylon's complete desolation (verses 19–22)

Babylon had been a magnificent and powerful city.

Yet Isaiah announced its total destruction, leaving it uninhabited and occupied by wild animals.

Henry sees the fulfillment of this prediction as evidence of Scripture's truth.

He also understands Babylon's ruin as a picture of the coming destruction of New Testament Babylon, and as a warning to all sinners to flee God's wrath.

For believers, it is encouragement to expect eventual victory over the enemies of their souls and of Christ's church.

Everything in the world can change and decay.

Let us therefore seek the kingdom that cannot be shaken and hold firmly to the grace through which we may serve God acceptably, with reverence and holy fear.

Verses 1-5 The threatenings of God's word press heavily upon the wicked, and are a sore burden, too heavy for them to bear. The persons brought together to lay Babylon waste, are called God's sanctified or appointed ones; designed for this service, and made able to do it. They are called God's mighty ones, because they had their might from God, and were now to use it for him. They come from afar. God can make those a scourge and ruin to his enemies, who are farthest off, and therefore least dreaded.
[Isa.13.6-Isa.13.18]
Verses 6-18 We have here the terrible desolation of Babylon by the Medes and Persians. Those who in the day of their peace were proud, and haughty, and terrible, are quite dispirited when trouble comes. Their faces shall be scorched with the flame. All comfort and hope shall fail. The stars of heaven shall not give their light, the sun shall be darkened. Such expressions are often employed by the prophets, to describe the convulsions of governments. God will visit them for their iniquity, particularly the sin of pride, which brings men low. There shall be a general scene of horror. Those who join themselves to Babylon, must expect to share her plagues, Rev. 18:4. All that men have, they would give for their lives, but no man's riches shall be the ransom of his life. Pause here and wonder that men should be thus cruel and inhuman, and see how corrupt the nature of man is become. And that little infants thus suffer, which shows that there is an original guilt, by which life is forfeited as soon as it is begun. The day of the Lord will, indeed, be terrible with wrath and fierce anger, far beyond all here stated. Nor will there be any place for the sinner to flee to, or attempt an escape. But few act as though they believed these things.
[Isa.13.19-Isa.13.22]
Verses 19-22 Babylon was a noble city; yet it should be wholly destroyed. None shall dwell there. It shall be a haunt for wild beasts. All this is fulfilled. The fate of this proud city is a proof of the truth of the Bible, and an emblem of the approaching ruin of the New Testament Babylon; a warning to sinners to flee from the wrath to come, and it encourages believers to expect victory over every enemy of their souls, and of the church of God. The whole world changes and is liable to decay. Wherefore let us give diligence to obtain a kingdom which cannot be moved; and in this hope let us hold fast that grace whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.

Babylon's downfall and the humiliation of its king (verses 1–23)

God governs the whole course of Providence with the good of his people in view.

Settlement in the promised land is a gift of his mercy.

Let the church welcome those whom God himself receives.

Wherever believers live, they should recommend true faith through upright, winsome conversation and conduct.

Those who formerly opposed them may eventually be humbled and brought to obedience—a pattern that can also be seen in the gospel's progress.

The Lord himself brings about this blessed change.

His people will find rest from sorrow, burdens and fear of further suffering.

Babylon possessed vast riches. Its king used his control of wealth to dominate other nations.

He had especially oppressed the Jews, increasing the guilt that would eventually bring judgment upon him.

Tyrants sacrifice their true interests to their passions and desires.

It is right to aspire to be like the Most Holy, because God commands us to be holy as he is holy.

But it is sinful to aspire to be like the Most High, demanding his supreme position for ourselves.

Satan used that ambition to tempt our first parents.

The proud monarch would be brought completely low.

Those who refuse to stop sinning may be stopped by God's judgment.

He would die and go down to the grave—the fate that ultimately overtakes even the greatest tyrants.

Genuine glory, meaning grace, accompanies the soul to heaven.

Earthly splendor descends with the body into the grave and comes to nothing.

Being denied an honorable burial for righteousness' sake can be borne with joy (Matthew 5:12).

But when disgrace is just punishment for sin, it points toward the final shame awaiting the unrepentant.

The fall of a tyrant can bring relief and joy to many people.

God will call to account those who destroy the peace of nations.

The picture of the king being received among the dead points, in Henry's reading, toward the world of departed spirits.

Human souls pass from this life into that world. They remain conscious there, although we cannot converse with them.

For someone who dies unholy after enjoying worldly glory and pleasure, death and judgment are dreadful indeed.

The offspring of persistent evildoers have no lasting honorable inheritance.

Babylon would become ruined and deserted.

Henry sees a further illustration of the destruction of New Testament Babylon (Revelation 18:2).

When people refuse to be cleansed through the broom of reformation, they face being swept away through the broom of destruction.

Assyria's power will be broken (verses 24–27)

Those who make themselves a burden and a yoke upon God's people should consider the judgment awaiting them.

Those who are called according to God's purpose may take comfort: everything God has determined will certainly stand.

The Lord of hosts had resolved to break Assyria's yoke.

His hand was raised to carry out that judgment, and no human power could turn it back.

Through such providential events, God demonstrates how deeply he hates sin.

The Philistines are warned (verses 28–32)

Isaiah also announced the destruction of Philistia through famine and war.

Henry says Hezekiah would become a more serious threat to them than Uzziah had been.

Their expectation of joy would end in mourning as their land suffered ruin.

The same warning applies to proud and rebellious sinners.

Yet the Lord founded Zion as a refuge for poor sinners who flee the judgment to come and trust in his mercy through Jesus Christ.

Let us tell others of the protection and comfort we have found, and urge them to seek that salvation too.

Verses 1-23 The whole plan of Divine Providence is arranged with a view to the good of the people of God. A settlement in the land of promise is of God's mercy. Let the church receive those whom God receives. God's people, wherever their lot is cast, should endeavour to recommend religion by a right and winning conversation. Those that would not be reconciled to them, should be humbled by them. This may be applied to the success of the gospel, when those were brought to obey it who had opposed it. God himself undertakes to work a blessed change. They shall have rest from their sorrow and fear, the sense of their present burdens, and the dread of worse. Babylon abounded in riches. The king of Babylon having the absolute command of so much wealth, by the help of it ruled the nations. This refers especially to the people of the Jews; and it filled up the measure of the king of Babylon's sins. Tyrants sacrifice their true interest to their lusts and passions. It is gracious ambition to covet to be like the Most Holy, for he has said, Be ye holy, for I am holy; but it is sinful ambition to aim to be like the Most High, for he has said, He who exalts himself shall be abased. The devil thus drew our first parents to sin. Utter ruin should be brought upon him. Those that will not cease to sin, God will make to cease. He should be slain, and go down to the grave; this is the common fate of tyrants. True glory, that is, true grace, will go up with the soul to heaven, but vain pomp will go down with the body to the grave; there is an end of it. To be denied burial, if for righteousness' sake, may be rejoiced in, Matt. 5:12. But if the just punishment of sin, it denotes that impenitent sinners shall rise to everlasting shame and contempt. Many triumphs should be in his fall. God will reckon with those that disturb the peace of mankind. The receiving the king of Babylon into the regions of the dead, shows there is a world of spirits, to which the souls of men remove at death. And that souls have converse with each other, though we have none with them; and that death and hell will be death and hell indeed, to all who fall unholy, from the height of this world's pomps, and the fulness of its pleasures. Learn from all this, that the seed of evil-doers shall never be renowned. The royal city is to be ruined and forsaken. Thus the utter destruction of the New Testament Babylon is illustrated, Rev. 18:2. When a people will not be made clean with the besom of reformation, what can they expect but to be swept off the face of the earth with the besom of destruction?
[Isa.14.24-Isa.14.27]
Verses 24-27 Let those that make themselves a yoke and a burden to God's people, see what they are to expect. Let those that are the called according to God's purpose, comfort themselves, that whatever God has purposed, it shall stand. The Lord of hosts has purposed to break the Assyrian's yoke; his hand is stretched out to execute this purpose; who has power to turn it back? By such dispensations of providence, the Almighty shows in the most convincing manner, that sin is hateful in his sight.
[Isa.14.28-Isa.14.32]
Verses 28-32 Assurance is given of the destruction of the Philistines and their power, by famine and war. Hezekiah would be more terrible to them than Uzziah had been. Instead of rejoicing, there would be lamentation, for the whole land would be ruined. Such destruction will come upon the proud and rebellious, but the Lord founded Zion for a refuge to poor sinners, who flee from the wrath to come, and trust in his mercy through Christ Jesus. Let us tell all around of our comforts and security, and exhort them to seek the same refuge and salvation.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The Divine judgments about to come upon the Moabites.

The destruction approaching Moab

Henry says this prophecy would be fulfilled within three years. Its fulfillment would confirm Isaiah's prophetic calling and support belief in the other messages he delivered.

The judgment announced against Moab unfolds in several ways.

Verse 1: The enemy would surprise the nation's principal cities. Terrible changes can come in a very short time.

Verse 2: The Moabites would seek help from their idols.

People without faith may find no genuine comforter when they suffer. Yet fear and disaster seldom lead them, by themselves, to come before the forgiving God with sincere sorrow and believing prayer.

Verse 3: Cries of grief would spread throughout the country.

It offers little relief to know that many other people share the same suffering.

Verse 4: Even Moab's soldiers would lose their courage.

God can quickly remove whatever a nation regards as its strongest protection.

Verse 5: The suffering would grieve people living nearby.

Although the Moabites were enemies of Israel, they were also fellow human beings. Their misery should still awaken compassion.

Verses 6–9: Isaiah describes widespread lamentation as Moab becomes prey to Assyria.

The country would be plundered, and famine would follow the devastation of war.

Those who dedicate themselves to gaining and storing up worldly possessions rarely consider how suddenly everything they possess may be taken away.

Let us warn even our enemies about the danger before them.

And as we warn them, pray that they may find forgiveness for their sins.

God can easily deprive a nation of that on which it most depended for strength and defence. 5. These calamities should cause grief in the neighbouring parts. Though enemies to Israel, yet as our fellow-creatures, it should be grievous to see them in such distress. In [Isa.15.6-Isa.15.9] Is. 15:6-9, the prophet describes the woful lamentations heard through the country of Moab, when it became a prey to the Assyrian army. The country should be plundered. Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesMoab is exhorted to yield obedience.1–5The pride and the judgments of Moab.6–14
Moab is called to submit and show mercy (verses 1–5)

God warns sinners how they can turn from the path of destruction. Here he gives such counsel to Moab.

The people were to send Judah the tribute they had previously agreed to pay.

Henry draws a wider lesson: turn away from sin through righteousness, and God may prolong peace.

He also applies the command to submission to Jesus Christ.

Give him your best gift—indeed, offer yourselves as a living sacrifice.

When you approach God, the supreme Ruler, come in the name of the Lamb of God.

Those refusing Christ's rule resemble a bird wandering away from its nest, exposed to the next bird of prey.

Anyone unwilling to reverence God becomes vulnerable to fear of everything else.

Moab was called to show kindness to the people of Israel.

Those who hope to receive help when they themselves suffer must show compassion to other sufferers.

The promise concerning Hezekiah's throne belongs, in an even greater sense, to the kingdom of Jesus Christ.

Serving him may not bring earthly riches, honor or public approval.

It may even expose believers to poverty and contempt.

Nevertheless, they gain peace of conscience and eternal life.

Moab's pride and judgment (verses 6–14)

Those who refuse all counsel cannot readily be helped.

Henry regards pride as especially destructive to souls.

Proud people often become easily angered, and their pride and anger lead to lies and fruitless schemes.

Moab's countryside was famous for fields and vineyards, yet invading armies would ruin them.

God can quickly turn laughter into mourning and joy into sorrow.

We should rejoice confidently in God, but receive earthly blessings with humble awareness that they may soon disappear.

The prophet felt sorrow at the destruction of such a beautiful and fruitful land.

Moab's false gods could provide no help.

But the God of Israel, the only true God, would fulfill everything he had declared.

Moab's coming judgment was close, and the people were urged to prepare.

Even the sternest warnings of God's wrath disclose a path of escape to those who take them seriously.

The only lasting escape is to submit to the Son of David and dedicate ourselves to him.

When the appointed time comes, the pride, prosperity and multitude of the wicked will all pass away.
classic_reading:
[Isa.16.1-Isa.16.5]

Moab is exhorted to yield obedience. ( [Isa.16.1-Isa.16.5] Is. 16:1-5) The pride and the judgments of Moab. ( [Isa.16.6-Isa.16.14] Is. 16:6-14)
Verses 1-5 God tells sinners what they may do to prevent ruin; so he does to Moab. Let them send the tribute they formerly engaged to pay to Judah. Take it as good advice. Break off thy sins by righteousness, it may lengthen thy quiet. And this may be applied to the great gospel duty of submission to Christ. Send him the lamb, the best you have, yourselves a living sacrifice. When you come to God, the great Ruler, come in the name of the Lamb, the Lamb of God. Those who will not submit to Christ, shall be as a bird that wanders from her nest, which shall be snatched up by the next bird of prey. Those who will not yield to the fear of God, shall be made to yield to the fear of every thing else. He advises them to be kind to the seed of Israel. Those that expect to find favour when in trouble themselves, must show favour to those in trouble. What is here said concerning the throne of Hezekiah, also belongs, in a much higher sense, to the kingdom of Jesus Christ. Though by subjection to Him we may not enjoy worldly riches or honours, but may be exposed to poverty and contempt, we shall have peace of conscience and eternal life.
[Isa.16.6-Isa.16.14]
Verses 6-14 Those who will not be counselled, cannot be helped. More souls are ruined by pride than by any other sin whatever. Also, the very proud are commonly very passionate. With lies many seek to gain the gratification of pride and passion, but they shall not compass proud and angry projects. Moab was famous for fields and vineyards; but they shall be laid waste by the invading army. God can soon turn laughter into mourning, and joy into heaviness. In God let us always rejoice with holy triumph; in earthly things let us always rejoice with holy trembling. The prophet looks with concern on the desolations of such a pleasant country; it causes inward grief. The false gods of Moab are unable to help; and the God of Israel, the only true God, can and will make good what he has spoken. Let Moab know her ruin is very near, and prepare. The most awful declarations of Divine wrath, discover the way of escape to those who take warning. There is no escape, but by submission to the Son of David, and devoting ourselves to him. And, at length, when the appointed time comes, all the glory, prosperity, and multitude of the wicked shall perish.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesSyria and Israel threatened.1–11The woe of Israel's enemies.12–14
Damascus and Israel brought low (verses 1–11)

Sin makes cities desolate.

It is strange that conquerors should glory in harming other human beings. Better for such ruined places to become grazing grounds for flocks than to shelter people openly rebelling against God and holiness.

Israel's fortresses and the northern kingdom would be brought down.

People who share in wrongdoing may rightly come to share in its consequences.

Israel's sins had made the people ripe for destruction.

Their former glory would be removed as quickly as grain disappears when a farmer harvests a field.

Nevertheless, God would preserve a small remnant.

Only a few would remain—one here and another there, as when fruit is left after harvest.

Those preserved would be brought toward holiness.

They would return to God, recognize his hand in events and give him his rightful praise.

This is the purpose of Providence under our Maker, and the work of grace under the Holy One of Israel.

The people would turn from idols, things they had invented through their own imaginations.

We have reason to regard as beneficial those trials that separate us from our sins.

God is the Rock of our salvation and our strength.

Forgetfulness of him lies at the root of every sin.

The pleasant plants and shoots imported from distant soil represent foreign and idolatrous forms of worship with their associated sinful practices.

People might cultivate those plants with great energy, but the effort would ultimately be wasted.

Let this picture teach the danger and unavoidable consequences of sin.

The Assyrian threat vanishes (verses 12–14)

The strength and rage of Assyria resembled enormous waves of the sea.

Yet once the God of Israel rebuked the invaders, they would flee like chaff before the wind.

In the evening, Jerusalem would be terrified by the presence of a powerful enemy.

By morning, the invading army would be almost entirely destroyed.

Happy are those who remember God as their salvation and depend on his power and grace.

The troubles believers endure, and the success their enemies enjoy, are both temporary.

But the lasting joy of God's people and the final defeat of those determined to destroy them will endure forever.

modern_osis:
Original heading

God's care for his people; and the increase of the church.

God's care for his church amid uncertain events

Henry describes this chapter as one of the most difficult passages in Scripture.

The people who first received it probably understood more of its details than readers do today.

Swift messengers travel by water toward a people singled out by Providence, measured and trampled down.

God's own people may also be trampled underfoot.

Yet those who imagine they can swallow up his people discover that, although the church may be brought low, she is not abandoned or finally destroyed.

All nations should watch the movements of God's Providence and follow the directions of his will.

The Lord gives Isaiah an assurance to pass on to his people.

Zion is his resting place forever.

He watches over it and provides comfort suited to the need of each moment.

That comfort is precious precisely because it comes at the proper time.

God will judge both his enemies and the enemies of his people.

His children enjoy his care in every season, while their enemies remain exposed to his judgment in every season.

This should bring us to offer a tribute of praise.

Whatever we bring to God must be offered in the way he has appointed.

We may expect to meet him where he has chosen to make his name known.

Through these events, the nations will recognize that the Lord is God and Israel belongs to him.

They too will unite in offering spiritual sacrifices for his glory.

Happy are those who take warning from God's judgments upon others and promptly join his people.

Whatever exact land or nation Isaiah has in view, the passage teaches us not to think God has forgotten his church or ceased to govern human affairs merely because he allows evil people to prevail for a while.

He has wise reasons that we cannot presently understand.

They will become clear at the great day of his appearing, when every human work is brought into judgment and everyone receives what is due.
classic_reading:
[Isa.18.1]
Chapter 18
God's care for his people; and the increase of the church.
This chapter is one of the most obscure in Scripture, though more of it probably was understood by those for whose use it was first intended, than by us now. Swift messengers are sent by water to a nation marked by Providence, and measured out, trodden under foot. God's people are trampled on; but whoever thinks to swallow them up, finds they are cast down, yet not deserted, not destroyed. All the dwellers on earth must watch the motions of the Divine Providence, and wait upon the directions of the Divine will. God gives assurance to his prophet, and by him to be given to his people. Zion is his rest for ever, and he will look after it. He will suit to their case the comforts and refreshments he provides for them; they will be acceptable, because seasonable. He will reckon with his and their enemies; and as God's people are protected at all seasons of the year, so their enemies are exposed at all seasons. A tribute of praise should be brought to God from all this. What is offered to God, must be offered in the way he has appointed; and we may expect him to meet us where he records his name. Thus shall the nations of the earth be convinced that Jehovah is the God, and Israel is his people, and shall unite in presenting spiritual sacrifices to his glory. Happy are those who take warning by his judgment on others, and hasten to join him and his people. Whatever land or people may be intended, we are here taught not to think that God takes no care of his church, and has no respect to the affairs of men, because he permits the wicked to triumph for a season. He has wise reasons for so doing, which we cannot now understand, but which will appear at the great day of his coming, when he will bring every work into judgment, and reward every man according to his works.

Egypt humbled through its own troubles (verses 1–17)

God would enter Egypt in judgment.

He would raise up the causes of Egypt's downfall from among its own people.

When ungodly people escape an immediate danger, they often imagine themselves safe.

But unless they repent, sin's consequences will pursue them and eventually overtake them.

The Egyptians would fall under a harsh ruler, a prediction Henry says was fulfilled soon afterward.

They were famous for learning and scientific skill.

Yet God would allow their wise men to follow corrupt plans and quarrel with one another, until the nation's own divisions made it an object of contempt and pity.

God can make sinners afraid of the very people they once looked down upon and oppressed.

He can also make evildoers terrify one another, while ordinary circumstances appear threatening on every side.

Egypt's future turning to the Lord (verses 18–25)

The prophetic words “In that day” do not always refer to the event described immediately before them.

Here Isaiah looks toward a later period.

Egyptians would learn to speak the holy language of Scripture, not merely recognizing it but using it.

Converting grace changes people's hearts, and therefore also changes their speech, because the mouth speaks from what fills the heart.

So many Jews would settle in Egypt, Henry says, that five cities would soon be filled.

A place formerly notorious for worshiping the sun would experience a remarkable spiritual reform.

Jesus Christ is the great Altar who makes the gifts offered through him acceptable.

There people would offer the gospel's spiritual sacrifices: prayer and praise.

Those wounded and humbled by God's correction should take courage.

When suffering leads them to return and call upon the Lord, he heals their souls and changes sorrowful petitions into joyful thanksgiving.

Gentile nations would be joined together within Christ's flock, under the great Shepherd.

They would also be united with the Jews.

All would be received by the same Lord and share the same blessing.

When believers meet at the same throne of grace and serve in the same work of worship, they should allow quarrels to end and be joined together through holy love.

Converting grace, by changing the heart, changes the language; for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. So many Jews shall come to Egypt, that they shall soon fill five cities. Where the sun was worshipped, a place infamous for idolatry, even there shall be a wonderful reformation. Christ, the great Altar, who sanctifies every gift, shall be owned, and the gospel sacrifices of prayer and praise shall be offered up. Let the broken-hearted and afflicted, whom the Lord has wounded, and thus taught to return to, and call upon him, take courage; for He will heal their souls, and turn their sorrowing supplications into joyful praises. They shall be owned together by him; they shall all share in one and the same blessing. Meeting at the same throne of grace, and serving with each other in the same business of religion, should end all disputes, and unite the hearts of believers to each other in holy love.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The invasion and conquest of Egypt and Ethiopia.

Isaiah's sign of the coming captivity

Isaiah became a sign to the people through his unusual clothing when he appeared in public.

As a prophet, he normally wore sackcloth, expressing his separation from worldly vanity.

God told him to remove it from his waist, to wear no outer garment and to walk barefoot.

This sign foretold that the king of Assyria would lead away captives from Egypt and Ethiopia in the same humiliated, stripped-down condition.

The world often judges believers foolish when their obedience to God makes them noticeably different from others.

But the Lord sustains his servants even when obedience involves particularly difficult trials.

What he asks them to endure for his sake is generally light when compared with the suffering that multitudes endure year after year through sin.

Whoever makes a created person or thing the foundation of hope, trust or pride—giving it the place belonging to God—will eventually be disappointed and ashamed.

Yet disappointment in human supports should not drive us to despair.

Instead it should drive us toward God, whose promises will not fail.

This same lesson remains important for us.

When the hour of urgent need arrives, where should we turn for help except to the Lord our Righteousness?
classic_reading:
[Isa.20.1]
Chapter 20
The invasion and conquest of Egypt and Ethiopia.
Isaiah was a sign to the people by his unusual dress, when he walked abroad. He commonly wore sackcloth as a prophet, to show himself mortified to the world. He was to loose this from his loins; to wear no upper garments, and to go barefooted. This sign was to signify, that the Egyptians and Ethiopians should be led away captives by the king of Assyria, thus stripped. The world will often deem believers foolish, when singular in obedience to God. But the Lord will support his servants under the most trying effects of their obedience; and what they are called upon to suffer for his sake, commonly is light, compared with what numbers groan under from year to year from sin. Those who make any creature their expectation and glory, and so put it in the place of God, will, sooner or later, be ashamed of it. But disappointment in creature-confidences, instead of driving us to despair, should drive us to God, and our expectation shall not be in vain. The same lesson is in force now; and where shall we look for aid in the hour of necessity, but to the Lord our Righteousness?
